Chapter 5: Challenging Modern Beliefs — Simplicity, Listening, and Trusting the Body
You know, the world of running can feel overwhelming sometimes. There’s advice everywhere—what to eat, how to train, which shoes are best. It’s easy to get caught up chasing the perfect formula, thinking that if you just find the right combination, you’ll finally reach your goals.
But when you look at the story of the Tarahumara, and even the science behind human endurance, you start to see a different way forward.
At the very center of the Tarahumara’s approach is simplicity. Their diet? It’s basic. Their gear? Minimal. And their training isn’t filled with strict plans and schedules—they just move, play, and let their bodies adapt along the way. Injuries? They’re rare, not because these runners avoid taking risks, but because they listen closely to what their bodies are telling them. They move naturally, and they trust that their bodies will get stronger as they go.
For a lot of modern runners, that idea can feel both freeing and a little bit scary. What if you let go of the belief that more is always better? More cushioning, more structure, more control—it’s what we’re told to look for. But what if, instead, you paid attention to how movement feels, not just how it’s supposed to look, or what the experts say you should do?
There’s one runner who tried just that. After years of frustrating injuries and setbacks, he decided to strip everything back. He swapped his high-tech shoes for simple sandals, started with short, easy runs, and stopped obsessing over his pace. At first, it felt pretty strange—almost like learning to run all over again. But over time, his body got used to it. The pain faded away, his stride grew lighter, and running started to feel effortless, maybe for the first time in his life.
Now, that doesn’t mean everyone needs to follow the exact same path. Every body is different, and what works for one person might not work for another. But there’s a powerful lesson here: trust your body’s wisdom. Movement is a natural part of being human, and your body is built for it—if you just give it the chance.
The same goes for nutrition. The Tarahumara thrive on a diet built around corn, beans, and vegetables, with a little meat and homemade drinks now and then. There’s no obsession with supplements or special products. It’s all about real food, shared with friends and family, and enjoyed without guilt or strict rules.
So, maybe the next time you’re tempted to complicate things, remember: sometimes, the simplest approach is the most powerful. Just listen, trust, and let your body do what it was designed to do.
